questions.title: How exactly does OFT guarantee hyperspherical energy preservation under orthogonal transformations?
questions.question_body: The paper defines the hyperspherical energy of a layer $W = \{w_1,\dots,w_n\} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}$ as $\mathrm{HE}(W) := \sum_{i \neq j} \lVert \hat{w}_i - \hat{w}_j \rVert^{-1}$ where $\hat{w}_i = w_i / \lVert w_i \rVert$. They claim that if we left-multiply by an orthogonal matrix $R \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ (i.e., $W' = R W$), the pairwise angles (and thus the hyperspherical energy) are preserved. Could someone provide a short derivation showing that $\angle(w_i, w_j) = \angle(Rw_i, Rw_j)$ implies $\lVert \hat{w}_i - \hat{w}_j \rVert = \lVert \widehat{Rw_i} - \widehat{Rw_j} \rVert$ and therefore $\mathrm{HE}(W') = \mathrm{HE}(W)$? Also, does the presence of bias vectors or subsequent nonlinearities affect this invariance claim at the layer level?

questions.title: Reconciling the two definitions of hyperspherical similarity and energy used in the paper
questions.question_body: Earlier, the paper motivates hyperspherical energy using "hyperspherical similarity (e.g., cosine similarity)" as a measure, but then defines the energy as $\mathrm{HE}(W)=\sum_{i \neq j}\lVert \hat{w}_i - \hat{w}_j \rVert^{-1}$. Since on the unit sphere $\lVert \hat{w}_i - \hat{w}_j \rVert^2 = 2(1-\cos\theta_{ij})$, this energy is a function of pairwise cosines but not equal to a sum of cosines. Why choose the inverse distance form rather than a direct function of $\cos\theta$ (e.g., $\sum_{i\neq j} -\cos\theta_{ij}$)? Does this specific form matter for the invariance and the empirical claims, or would any strictly monotone function of the angle suffice?

questions.title: Is OFT merely a change of basis for the inputs, and does that limit its expressivity?
questions.question_body: For a linear layer with pretrained weights $W^0$, OFT uses $z = (R W^0)^\top x$. Algebraically this equals $z = (W^0)^\top (R^\top x)$, i.e., applying $R^\top$ to the input feature before the pretrained weights. Does this mean OFT is just a learned reparameterization of the input basis for that layer? If so, how does OFT achieve task-specific adaptation across the entire network when non-linearities, residual connections, and cross-attention are present? Is there a subtlety because $R$ is different per layer (and not absorbed globally), so the composition cannot be reduced to a single global basis change?

questions.title: Clarifying which UNet attention weights receive OFT and how $R$ is shared
questions.question_body: The paper says "to compare fairly to LoRA, we only apply OFT to finetune the attention weights" in Stable Diffusion v1.5. Which specific matrices per attention block are transformed: $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$, and/or $W_O$? Is a distinct orthogonal $R$ learned per matrix and per layer, or shared among some of them (e.g., shared across $Q$, $K$, $V$ or across blocks at the same resolution)? How is the dimensionality $d$ in $R \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ chosen relative to the head dimension, number of heads, and concatenation layout?

questions.title: Does re-scaled OFT truly leave hyperspherical energy unchanged?
questions.question_body: In the re-scaled variant, the forward pass is $z = (R W^0 D)^\top x$ where $D = \mathrm{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_n)$ rescales columns (neurons) and $s_i > 0$. Since $\mathrm{HE}(W)$ uses normalized columns $\hat{w}_i = w_i/\lVert w_i \rVert$, my understanding is that column-wise scaling by $D$ cancels out in $\hat{w}_i$, so $\mathrm{HE}(R W^0 D) = \mathrm{HE}(R W^0)$. Is this always true even when some columns are zero or nearly zero? Are there any practical caveats (e.g., numerical stability) that could make $D$ inadvertently affect the computed energy or the angle preservation claim?

questions.title: Cayley parameterization details: determinant, stability, and constraints in COFT
questions.question_body: The orthogonal matrix is parameterized as $R = (I + Q)(I - Q)^{-1}$ with a skew-symmetric $Q = -Q^\top$. The paper states this generates only matrices with determinant $1$. I thought the Cayley map excludes orthogonals with eigenvalue $-1$, thus it parameterizes a subset of $SO(d)$ (with $\det=1$), not all of it. Is that the intended meaning? Also, since COFT imposes a constraint $\lVert R - I \rVert \le \epsilon$, the paper approximates $R \approx I + 2Q + \mathcal{O}(Q^2)$ and then constrains $\lVert Q \rVert \le \epsilon'$. Which norm is used in practice (spectral, Frobenius), and how do you ensure the Neumann series converges (e.g., $\lVert Q \rVert < 1$)? Any advice to avoid numerical instabilities from $(I - Q)^{-1}$ during training?

questions.title: How should I interpret the block-diagonal $R$ for convolution layers?
questions.question_body: For fully connected layers with $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}$, left-multiplication by $R \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ transforms the input feature basis. For convolution weights, say $W \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\text{out}} \times C_{\text{in}} \times k \times k}$, what is the precise mapping for $R$ (shape, axes) when using a block-diagonal structure with $r$ blocks? If $r = C_{\text{in}}$, you mention an interpretation akin to depth-wise transformations. Could you detail the exact tensor contractions or reshaping steps so it is clear which dimension plays the role of $d$ and which plays $n$ when bringing conv kernels into the $d \times n$ view?

questions.title: When is OFT actually more parameter-efficient than LoRA?
questions.question_body: The paper compares LoRA parameters $r'(d+n)$ versus OFT block-diagonal parameters $\tfrac{d}{2}(d/r - 1)$. Depending on $d,n,r,r'$, LoRA can be smaller or larger. In typical SD v1.5 attention layers (with head dimension $d_h$ and number of heads $h$), could you provide concrete parameter counts for common settings (e.g., $d_h \in \{64, 80\}$, $h \in \{8, 12\}$) to show when OFT is smaller? Also, the comparison assumes $r$ and $r'$ scale with $d$ (e.g., $r=r'=\alpha d$). Is that assumption necessary? How should one choose $r$ in practice to balance efficiency and performance?

questions.title: Rank and update structure: how does $(R - I)W^0$ compare to LoRA’s low-rank update?
questions.question_body: The paper rewrites $RW^0 = W^0 + (R - I)W^0$ and notes an analogy to LoRA’s additive low-rank update. Since $\operatorname{rank}((R - I)W^0) \le \min\{\operatorname{rank}(R - I), \operatorname{rank}(W^0)\}$ and typically $\operatorname{rank}(W^0)$ is full, the rank is bounded by $\operatorname{rank}(R - I)$. For a block-diagonal $R$ with $r$ blocks, can we bound $\operatorname{rank}(R - I)$ in terms of $r$ and $d$? Under what settings does OFT’s effective update behave like a genuinely low-rank update versus a full-rank but structured update?

questions.title: COFT’s $\epsilon$ constraint: what norm is used and how should $\epsilon$ be set?
questions.question_body: COFT constrains $\lVert R - I \rVert \le \epsilon$ and then replaces this with $\lVert Q \rVert \le \epsilon'$ using the approximation $R \approx I + 2Q + \mathcal{O}(Q^2)$. In practice: (1) Which norm is used for $\lVert \cdot \rVert$ (spectral, Frobenius), (2) how do you select $\epsilon$ or $\epsilon'$ across different layers with different $d$, and (3) how sensitive are results to this choice? Any recommended schedules to anneal or tune $\epsilon$ during training for stability?

questions.title: Toy autoencoder experiment: what exactly are the 'magnitude-only' and 'angle-only' computations?
questions.question_body: In Figure 1 (toy autoencoder), training uses standard inner products $z = w^\top x$. At test time you compare: (a) the same inner product, (b) "magnitude information", and (c) "angular information" (cosine). Could you formalize (b) and (c)? For example, is (c) implemented as $z = \frac{w^\top x}{\lVert w \rVert \lVert x \rVert}$ and (b) as $z = \lVert w \rVert \lVert x \rVert$ (or something else)? Also, are feature maps rescaled or shifted to the range expected by downstream layers, and how is reconstruction fair across the three variants?

questions.title: Why does 'OFT without orthogonality' fail so catastrophically in your ablation?
questions.question_body: Figure 3 suggests that relaxing the orthogonality constraint (i.e., learning a general linear transform instead of an orthogonal one) leads to failure. Is the failure due to optimization issues (e.g., ill-conditioned matrices leading to exploding/vanishing signals) or due to semantic drift from not preserving angles? Did you try additional regularizations such as spectral norm constraints, weight decay on the transform, or small-step constraints that might stabilize a general linear transform without enforcing exact orthogonality?

questions.title: Control consistency metrics: implementation specifics and potential biases
questions.question_body: For controllable generation, you propose a control consistency evaluation: estimate the control signal from the generated image and compare to the input control. Could you specify the exact off-the-shelf models and settings used for each task? For C2I, which edge detector and thresholds compute IoU/F1? For S2I, which semantic segmentation model, label set, and resolution are used for mIoU/mean/overall accuracy? For L2F, which landmark detector and what normalization are used in the mean $\ell_2$ distance? Do these choices bias metrics toward/against certain visual styles produced by different methods?

questions.title: Compositionality of multiple OFT adapters: how would $R$'s be combined across tasks?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions a potential for compositionality: orthogonal matrices from multiple OFT finetunings can be multiplied and remain orthogonal. Concretely, if I have two downstream tasks yielding $R^{(A)}$ and $R^{(B)}$ for the same layer, is the composed adapter $R^{(B)}R^{(A)}$ expected to preserve both task adaptations when multiplied into $W^0$? In practice, are $R$'s trained on disjoint tasks likely to commute, or can order matter substantially? Any initial evidence (positive or negative) for catastrophic interference when composing multiple $R$'s?

questions.title: No inference overhead claim: any caveats when pre-multiplying $R$ into $W^0$?
questions.question_body: The paper states there is no inference overhead because one can precompute $W = R W^0$ and discard $R$. Are there scenarios where $R$ was shared across multiple layers or blocks such that pre-multiplication changes memory layout or weight tying in unexpected ways? Also, when using block sharing across $R$ blocks, does this impact how you fold $R$ into $W^0$ if multiple layers share the same $R$ parameters (e.g., you would still materialize separate $W$ per layer, losing the sharing at inference)?

questions.title: Why is minimizing hyperspherical energy harmful for finetuning diffusion models?
questions.question_body: The paper contrasts OFT with prior work that minimizes hyperspherical energy in classification, arguing that minimizing energy during finetuning would "destroy the original semantic structures" in diffusion models. Could you elaborate on the intuition or provide an example? If $\mathrm{HE}(W)$ (sum of inverse distances) gets minimized, neurons become more uniformly spread on the sphere, reducing redundancy. Why does that uniformization particularly damage the pretrained generative semantics in diffusion UNets, whereas it is beneficial in classification backbones?

questions.title: Practical guidance on choosing the number of blocks $r$ for block-diagonal $R$
questions.question_body: Block-diagonal $R = \mathrm{diag}(R_1,\dots,R_r)$ trades off parameter-efficiency and flexibility. Is there a heuristic for picking $r$ per layer (e.g., proportional to $d$, aligned with channel groups or heads)? Does sharing blocks ($R_i = R_j$) significantly hurt performance in practice? Any empirical results showing performance vs. $r$ curves on subject-driven and controllable generation to guide practitioners?
